extracted.intended_audience: employers, workers, labor advocates, attorneys, state attorneys general, and other stakeholders affected by DOL rulemaking on independent contractor classification under the FLSA
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for drafting, evaluating, and deciding a Department of Labor regulation replacing the 2021 independent-contractor rule under the Fair Labor Standards Act, including consideration of alternatives, statutory precedent, and anticipated effects on misclassification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduce misclassification and restore totality-of-the-circumstances analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: The rulemaking is motivated in part by the assessment that rescinding and replacing the 2021 IC Rule will likely both reduce misclassification and restore the Department's ability to consider all relevant facts under a totality-of-the-circumstances economic reality test.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department believes the 2021 IC Rule increased the risk of misclassification by introducing confusion and narrowing the inquiry; the replacement should allow full consideration of relevant facts to protect workers and ensure fair competition among businesses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not predetermine weight of factors; avoid elevating/devaluing factors
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department will not predetermine the weight of certain factors or elevate some as 'core' in a way that limits consideration of other relevant facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 2021 IC Rule improperly narrowed the test by elevating certain factors and precluding consideration of certain facts; the final rule must avoid those approaches to prevent misunderstanding and misapplication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Align regulatory guidance with Supreme Court and federal appellate precedent
rubrics_metrics.description: The final rule should be consistent with the text of the FLSA and decades of judicial precedent interpreting the Act, grounding the economic realities analysis in federal appellate case law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department emphasizes that the Supreme Court has applied an 'economic reality' standard and rejected tests relying on isolated or dispositive factors; regulations should reflect that precedent to improve consistency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use a multifactor economic reality (totality-of-the-circumstances) test
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply a nonexhaustive multifactor economic realities analysis in which there is no presumption of employee status, no one factor is determinative, and all relevant factors must be considered and weighed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This approach contrasts with ABC-style or common-law control tests; the Department frames the factors consistent with circuits' analyses and emphasizes weighing multiple considerations together.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject adoption of an ABC test for FLSA worker status
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department declines to adopt an ABC test because it is inconsistent with Supreme Court precedent and would presume employee status unless employers meet three dispositive criteria.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An ABC test assumes workers are employees absent proof to the contrary and treats isolated factors as independently determinative—an approach the Department views as incompatible with the FLSA and controlling case law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject adoption of the common law control test
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department rejects adopting a common law control test because it would be contrary to the 'suffer or permit' language of section 3(g) of the FLSA and is too narrow to protect workers under the Act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts and the Department view the common law control test as inconsistent with the broader statutory definition of 'employ' that Congress intended for the FLSA.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer formal regulation over subregulatory guidance for clarity and accessibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt detailed federal regulations (rather than only subregulatory guidance) because regulatory text is easier for stakeholders to locate and read and is more robust for aligning with precedent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulations allow formal notice-and-comment, may improve consistency among courts, and centralize guidance so employers and workers need not search disparate WHD guidance and court cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider and explain alternatives (including less disruptive options) per the APA
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department must consider reasonable alternatives to the proposed action (e.g., retaining aspects of the 2021 rule, adopting common-law or ABC tests, partial rescission, or issuing subregulatory guidance) and explain why alternatives are accepted or rejected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department considered four alternatives and explained why some (common law, ABC) are legally inconsistent with precedent and why partial rescission was insufficient because of the 2021 Rule's tensions with judicial precedent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not delay rulemaking pending extended court application or additional data when harms exceed benefits
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department may proceed with rescission and replacement without waiting for courts to apply the prior rule or for more data, when continued application of the prior rule risks exacerbating confusion and misclassification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters urged delay; the Department finds those timing arguments unpersuasive given demonstrated departures from precedent and the potential for ongoing harms if the 2021 IC Rule remains in effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for stakeholder reliance and regulatory whiplash but weigh against statutory and precedent concerns
rubrics_metrics.description: While recognizing added costs and uncertainty from changing rules (the 'regulatory whiplash'), the Department evaluates such reliance arguments against the need to align with the FLSA and judicial precedent and to prevent worker harm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some commenters cited disruption to businesses; the Department acknowledges impacts but found the benefits of correcting the 2021 Rule's departures from precedent outweigh those concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid industry-specific rebuttable presumptions of employee status
rubrics_metrics.description: Decline recommendations to adopt rebuttable presumptions (e.g., that construction workers are employees) because such industry-specific presumptions would be inconsistent with Supreme Court and appellate precedent and with the intended general analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department's objective is a general analysis applicable across industries rather than targeted presumptions that would conflict with precedent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure regulatory text does not narrow the set of facts courts may consider
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulations must not limit the facts that may be considered in applying the economic reality test; the final rule rejects formulations that 'narrowed the economic reality test by limiting the facts that may be considered.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Partial rescission that left in place 2021 Rule descriptions of factors was rejected because those descriptions were in tension with judicial precedent and unduly constrained fact consideration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ground the rule in the Department's expertise and enforcement responsibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department asserts it has relevant expertise and authority to interpret the Act and issue regulatory guidance on what constitutes an employment relationship under the FLSA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rulemaking rationale references decades of DOL experience administering and enforcing the FLSA and the agency's authority that 'comes with its authority to administer and enforce the Act.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Publish accessible commentary to explain how each factor informs the economic dependence analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: The commentary to the rule should clarify how each factor helps answer whether a worker is in business for themself or economically dependent on an employer, to reduce confusion inherent in a multifactor balancing test.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Several commenters supported explanatory commentary recognizing that multifactor tests can cause confusion without clarification of how factors inform the analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain and document why certain alternatives are legally nonviable
rubrics_metrics.description: When considering alternatives such as adopting an ABC test or a common law test, the rule must explain their inconsistency with Supreme Court precedent and thus their legal nonviability in this context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department repeatedly explains that such alternatives either conflict with the FLSA's 'suffer or permit' standard or with the Supreme Court's economic reality jurisprudence.
